prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part base editing prize for Liu, Komor and Gaudelli. After round 1 the question is not whether base editing has defined chemistry, since all three members who engaged with it accept that, but whether it is distinct from 2020 and attributable. On distinctness, the 2020 prize recognised programmable cleavage of DNA by Cas9; base editing is a different chemical operation, a deaminase tethered to a nickase or dead Cas protein that rewrites one base without a double-strand break, and the adenine editor required directed evolution of TadA to create an activity that does not exist in nature. That is deaminase engineering, which is what a chemistry citation should say. On attribution, the citation I propose names the two founding classes of editor and the laboratory that conceived and drove the programme, which is a defensible and explainable story for a broad audience. It also has the broadest opening support, many independent replications, and clinical benefit in patients.
statement.case_against: Three reservations remain real and I do not dismiss them. First, six years separate base editing from the 2020 prize, and Aili and Sparr are right that a committee could prefer to let genome editing settle, possibly into a later combined recognition with prime editing. Second, Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID was independent and near-contemporaneous for cytosine editing, and the three-name limit, not scientific merit, excludes them; Somfai's Liu-only variant reduces that exposure but at the price of an unequal recognition of the founding inventors. Third, long-term safety, bystander editing and off-target deamination are still being characterised, and no base-editing therapy is yet approved as far as I can state with confidence.

responses.point: Somfai supports a Liu-only base editing part so that Buchwald and Hartwig can share the three-person limit in a two-part prize with Pd-catalysed C-N coupling.
responses.response: I accept your point that the deaminase-nickase fusion answers the overlap worry, and that Target-AID makes a three-name base editing prize contestable. I do not move to Liu alone. The adenine editor is a separate invention from the cytosine editor, made by directed evolution of TadA in Gaudelli's work, and a citation about base editing as a chemical class would be incomplete without both inventors. I also cannot explain to a general audience why C-N coupling and DNA editing belong in one prize; you concede they share no theme, and the opening support for B065 was thin. The limit is a constraint on credit, not a reason to dilute a coherent citation.

responses.point: Aili ranks B011 first and argues that degradation is a more novel modality than base editing, while saying that if a Liu-centred prize is chosen the case should rest on deaminase engineering and evolution chemistry, not on clinical promise.
responses.response: I agree with your framing instruction and have rewritten my case accordingly: the citation is about the chemistry of base conversion and the evolved deaminases. On novelty I am not persuaded that degradation clearly wins. The bifunctional concept is from 2001 but the drug-like chemistry and the cereblon glue mechanism came later from different people, so the committee would have to choose among three separable discoveries, and the question I put in round 1 about which approved degrader proves the modality has not been answered by anyone. That keeps B011 as my first alternative, not my preferred part.

responses.point: Aqvist weights B011 as the only candidate ranked by all eight members and says breadth matters more to him than first places, while also pressing that condensate maturity is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with you on B046: my own maturity doubt is the same, and I do not move it above my alternative slot. On breadth I would separate acceptance from preference. B011 was ranked by everyone but is ranked anywhere from first to eighth, and two of your three named laureates would leave out the cereblon line that several of us regard as the mechanistic centre. Breadth that is partly low ranking does not tell us which citation we can write. I would want the committee to say precisely what B011's citation covers before treating it as a consensus candidate.

responses.point: Chabes supports the same Liu, Komor and Gaudelli trio on the grounds of explicit enzymatic chemistry, and asks that attribution of Target-AID be handled openly.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration. On your request for precision, I would say in the committee record that Nishida and Kondo reported cytosine base editing independently and at nearly the same time, that the adenine editor has no counterpart in their work, and that the exclusion follows the three-name limit. That is the strongest honest statement I can make from what I hold, and I would rather have it written down than depend on a date comparison I cannot fully verify.

responses.point: Zou proposes perovskite absorbers (Miyasaka, Snaith, Park) and argues that a prize should recognise the discovery and not wait for engineering deployment.
responses.response: I agree with your principle that a prize recognises a discovery and not deployment, and I applied it to base editing myself. My difficulty with B047 is the attribution rather than the maturity: the 2012 solid-state step is shared with Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis, and I cannot give a three-name citation that I could defend as complete. If a narrower citation on the absorber class could be agreed, I would revisit it, but I do not see that agreement forming here.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards base editing as sufficiently distinct from, and far enough after, the 2020 CRISPR prize.
Whether Target-AID priority is strong enough that a Liu, Komor and Gaudelli citation would be judged unfair to Kondo and Nishida.
Whether any base-editing therapy has been approved, and how much weight the committee should give clinical benefit not yet confirmed in an approved product.
Whether PROTAC and molecular-glue credit can be fitted into one citation that does not read as slighting Handa, Ito and Gray.
Whether condensate biology has quantitative criteria mature enough for a chemistry prize.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1: no conflict with any shortlisted ballot ID is apparent. I share a Lund affiliation with Peter Somfai and Emma Sparr, and my own research on quantum-dot thermoelectrics and molecular motors does not overlap with any shortlisted candidate, so no recusal is indicated.
